title: The Pale
hook: the Russian Empire confines most Jews to its western provinces

segments.voice: Yesterday, Volozhin: two students over one book, sharpening each other like iron. Your line was the yeshiva. Did you learn something with someone instead of alone? Today, the map that yeshiva sat on. Day nine hundred sixty-eight.

A Jewish trader has goods to sell in a city a few days' ride to the east. The roads are open. The horse is ready. The buyers are waiting. And he cannot simply go. No wall stands in his way, and no river. The line he cannot cross is written in a law, drawn on a map in an office far away. On one side, he may live, trade, marry and be buried. On the other side, for him, the road ends, unless an official grants a permit he may never get. His Christian neighbor can take that road tomorrow. Today, a boundary with a name: the Pale.
screen: `A ROAD THAT IS OPEN.` → `A LINE WRITTEN IN A LAW.` → `ON THE OTHER SIDE, THE ROAD ENDS.`

segments.voice: When the Russian Empire took over lands that had belonged to Poland, it took over the Jewish communities living there too, the world of the Council of Four Lands and the Baal Shem Tov and the Vilna Gaon. The empire's answer was a boundary. Jews were, with some exceptions, allowed to live only in its western provinces, and kept out of the Russian heartland and its great cities. That region came to be called the Pale of Settlement. Inside it, life was crowded and often poor, but it was also full: market towns, study houses, Hasidic courts, the yeshiva at Volozhin from yesterday. A whole Yiddish-speaking world grew up inside a line someone else had drawn. In Hebrew and Yiddish the Pale had a name of its own, techum ha-moshav, the boundary of settlement. And that word techum, boundary, already meant something in Jewish life. It is the word for the limit on how far a person walks on Shabbat. It goes back to a verse about the manna in the wilderness. In the JPS translation of Exodus, the Israelites are told: "abide ye every man in his place, let no man go out of his place on the seventh day." The rabbis read that as a measured distance around a town, a Shabbat boundary. So Jews in the Pale knew two kinds of boundary by the same name. One was chosen, taken on as holy rest, and it lifted every week when Shabbat ended. The other was imposed, by a government that did not want them, and it did not lift at sunset. Same word. Opposite meaning. One limit was a gift you kept. The other was a fence kept around you.
screen: `THE EMPIRE DRAWS A LINE.` · `A WHOLE WORLD INSIDE IT.` · `TECHUM — THE SHABBAT BOUNDARY.` · then, large: `ONE CHOSEN, ONE IMPOSED.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: notice a freedom of movement you have. Sit, and let your feet rest flat on the floor. Feel them there. Now think of where those feet can take you this week without asking anyone's permission. The store. A friend's street. Another town. Another country, maybe, with a passport in a drawer. Let one of those places come clearly to mind. Then, gently, remember the trader at the edge of the Pale, with his horse ready and nowhere to ride. Hold both pictures. You don't have to do anything with them. The bell holds the time.
The Pale. The Pale of Settlement, the western provinces of the Russian Empire where Jews were, with some exceptions, required to live. In Hebrew, techum ha-moshav. Today's word.
Your line: the pale. Today, when you go somewhere, a shop, a street, a city, notice for one moment that nobody drew a line to stop you. Day nine hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Jews who keep Shabbat by traditional law observe the techum, staying within a set walking distance of the town where they spend the day.

fork.setup: you're a Jewish trader at the edge of the Pale, with buyers waiting in a city beyond it. what does the law allow?
options: ride on, like your Christian neighbor.
stay inside the line, unless you belong to an exception the law allows.
move your whole family east for good.
fork.reveal: Jews were, with some exceptions, required to live inside the Pale, and kept out of the Russian heartland.

original.note: Hebrew: boundary. The Pale was techum ha-moshav; the Shabbat walking limit is techum Shabbat.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Pale was just an old name for a region.
what it means: a legal boundary in the Russian Empire, inside which Jews were, with some exceptions, required to live.
what a scholar hears: its Hebrew name used techum, the same word as the Shabbat boundary drawn from Exodus 16:29.

notes: Claims rule: no dates or population figures are given; the index hook's 'most Jews' is rendered as 'with some exceptions'. Please confirm the description of the Pale and its exceptions.

Exodus 16:29 JPS 1917 wording: please verify exactly ('abide ye every man in his place, let no man go out of his place on the seventh day').
The rabbinic derivation of techum Shabbat from Exodus 16:29: please confirm the framing and the Mishnah/Talmud reference (Eruvin).
The trader scene is illustrative, not a documented individual.

Audit: the hook said flatly that the trader 'cannot go'; the Pale restricted residence, and Jews could at times travel or stay beyond it by permit or exemption (e.g. some merchants). Softened to 'cannot simply go' and 'unless an official grants a permit he may never get'.
